doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Dizzy Gillespie in the sextet
summary: Carter says Gillespie was far advanced and that the sextet used small arrangements, originals and pop tunes, none recorded.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Can you talk about Dizzy at this time and what impression he made on you or what he was doing musically that might have been different?

Well, what he was doing musically was certainly far advanced, and what he was doing on the instrument was, gee, unlike anything that we’d ever heard on the instrument then, things that you wouldn’t think were possible. But he didn’t know they were impossible, so he did them, you know, and he still does them. But, you know, what do you say about Dizzy that hasn’t been said before?
Were there things that you frankly didn’t understand, that didn’t sound right to you, or did everything make sense that he was . . .

I don’t know. I don’t remember my first impression. I mean, I can’t say that it didn’t sound right to me. It sounded different. I mean, the fact that I hired him for my sextet certainly shows that I must have appreciated what he was doing. But gee, I don’t know. Dizzy is Dizzy, and he was and he is.
This sextet, what sort of music were you playing? Were there arrangements for the group that you did?
Yeah, there were some small arrangements.
Do you remember any of the repertoire, because this is another one of these tragedies, that nothing was ever recorded or even broadcast by that group.
Well, if it wasn’t recorded and wasn’t broadcast, I wouldn’t remember it.
Yeah, there were some originals, yeah, and some popular tunes, you know.
Did Dizzy contribute anything as far as . . .
Not to my book at that time, no.
